pending_articles.title: LIF is a pro-algesic mediator in human and mouse models of arthritis-related pain
pending_articles.content: Purpose: Emerging clinical and experimental data suggest that JAK inhibitors (JAKi) are effective in reducing pain in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). We recently showed that JAK/STAT signalling cytokines, specifically IL-6, LIF and IL-11, are present in the RA joint and can act directly on human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived sensory neurons by increasing their STAT3 phosphorylation (pSTAT3) levels and expression of select pain-relevant genes. In this study, we determined that LIF is the most consequential cytokine out of the three, altering neuronal signalling, outgrowth and pain-like behaviours in in vitro and in vivo models of arthritis. Methods: Human iPSC-derived sensory neurons were stimulated with RA synovial fluid (SF) or with cytokine-treated RA synovial fibroblast conditioned media (CM) in the absence or presence of anti-cytokine antibodies. pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 levels, and gene expression patterns, were assessed by Western blot and RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq). The immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6) was assessed for LIF-induced JAK/STAT signalling in addition to neurite outgrowth assays as a functional readout of the sensory neurons. Lastly, mouse models were used to assess pain-related behaviours in vivo. Results: LIF was found to be consistently present in the SF from painful joints from individuals with inflammatory arthritis. Western blotting revealed that the addition of RA SF to iPSC-derived sensory neurons led to LIF-dependent induction of pSTAT3 and pSTAT1, while RNA-seq demonstrated that LIF alters the transcriptome of sensory neurons more prominently than IL-6 and IL-11, up-regulating signature genes related to peripheral neuron sensitization, such as TRPV1, NTRK1, BDNF, HRH1 and SCN10A. Similarly, cytokine-treated fibroblast conditioned media was shown to induce neuronal pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 and upregulate expression of BDNF, HRH1 and VGF in a LIF-dependent manner. Additionally, the immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6), which also exhibited LIF-induced pSTAT1 and pSTAT3, showed increased neurite outgrowth after axotomy when treated with LIF. Finally, in a mouse model of inflammatory arthritis, LIF was shown to be significantly increased in the affected joint. Furthermore, intraarticular injection of LIF into a healthy mouse knee resulted in increased responsiveness to painful pressure stimuli in that joint. Conclusions: Our data indicate that LIF may be a pro-algesic mediator and a possible therapeutic target to improve pain management in individuals living with inflammatory arthritis.

pending_articles.title: Real-Time Neurotransmitter Sensing in Midbrain Organoids Using 3D Carbon Cup Electrodes
pending_articles.content: Real time, chemically selective detection of neurotransmitter release in brain organoids remains a challenge due to their complex three dimensional architecture and limited optical accessibility. We introduce 3D printed carbon cup electrodes (CCEs) -pyrolyzed, multi level pillar structures - designed to confine a single organoid, increase electroactive surface area, and enable amperometric recordings of oxidizable neurotransmitters. The CCEs exhibit excellent electrochemical performance and reproducibility, supporting diffusion controlled dopamine redox behavior without interference from culture medium. Using ventral midbrain (vMB) organoids at two maturation stages (Day 30 and Day 90), we demonstrate real time detection of potassium evoked dopamine release directly from organoids. Mature organoids exhibit higher peak currents, correlating with increased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression confirmed by immunocytochemistry. Embedding organoids in Matrigel significantly attenuates dopamine signals, indicating a diffusion barrier that limits stimulant access and/or dopamine transport to the electrode. Repetitive stimulations reveal progressive depletion of dopamine stores, consistent with diminished vesicular release. Chemical perturbations using 6 hydroxydopamine and verapamil further validate the platform by producing substantial reductions in dopamine release accompanied by loss of TH neurons. These results establish CCEs as a powerful tool for label free, real-time monitoring of neurotransmission in human organoids, with potential for multiplexed sensing and integration of enzymatic detection strategies for non electroactive neurotransmitters.

pending_articles.title: Adolescent prodromal phenotypes of psychiatric disorders: insights from a novel DISC1-perturbed monkey model
pending_articles.content: Neurodevelopmental deficits frequently lead to mild but significant adolescent social and cognitive changes, representing prodromal manifestations of adult-onset psychiatric disorders in a cross-disease manner. Although experimental medicine utilizes animal models to address the mechanisms, rodent brains lack critical structures for human higher brain functions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. To fill this translational gap, we generated monkeys with an impaired DISC1 gene locus, targeting the multifunctional protein essential for neurodevelopment and involved in transdiagnostic mental health risks. Here we analyze the F0 animals by minimizing mosaicism. At ages equivalent to human adolescence, these monkeys exhibited blunted responsiveness to social stimuli and increased internal drives, mirroring altered social behaviors in the prodromal stage in humans. Resting-state functional MRI data indicated disrupted global functional connectivity and reorganization of network topology, marked by a shift in the dominance of brain hubs from prefrontal regions to sensory areas. This primate model provides a unique platform for studying psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, across the developmental trajectory.

pending_articles.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
pending_articles.content: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory. Net excitatory input onto this population decreased, most strongly that from older-memory populations, which allowed inputs of older memories to drive their own neurons again. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: plasticity is confined to one population, whose neurons lose inputs that are silent when they fire. The mechanism held under Dale's law, and depression of excitatory synapses alone, without any inhibitory plasticity, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation and highlight the potential for integrating human-like learning behaviors into artificial neural networks.

pending_articles.title: Temporal tuning of actin nucleation by the repurposed DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 encodes distinct axon guidance decisions
pending_articles.content: Axon guidance is essential for neural circuit assembly and function. While much of the repertoire of guidance cues and receptors is known, its limited diversity cannot fully explain the remarkable complexity of the brain connectome. How temporally ordered, context-dependent intrinsic programs shape the diversity of axonal responses to guidance signals remains poorly understood. We reveal how non-canonical Wnt5a signalling repurposes the DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 as a downstream integrator to control retinal ganglion cell axon decision-making at the midline. We demonstrate that differential RAD51/fignl1 expression and interaction dynamics between ipsilateral and contralateral axons tunes the magnitude and temporal dynamics of F-actin nucleation, thereby encoding their trajectory choice. Our findings establish temporal control of cytoskeletal dynamics as a key determinant of axon decision-making and thereby a fundamental layer of circuit wiring. They provide a potential mechanistic framework linking mutations in the DNA repair gene RAD51 to neurodevelopmental disorders with midline guidance defects.

pending_articles.title: Sex shapes capillary flows and oxygen extraction in the middle-aged mouse brain
pending_articles.content: Sex differences in brain aging are well documented, but their origin within the cerebrovascular hierarchy remains unclear. Here we show that cortical blood flow is higher in female than male mice at 15 months of age, at a point when an earlier sex difference in pulsatility and resistance indices has already converged, pial vessel diameter shows no difference between sexes, and estrogen levels are similar between sexes. Using an indicator-dilution and intravascular oxygen measurements using two-photon microscopy, we found that capillary transit-time heterogeneity (CTH) scales more steeply with mean transit time in females, consistent with a passively regulated capillary network, and that this is accompanied by reduced oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) without deficit in arterial oxygen delivery. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that sex differences are organized into distinct regional programs, most prominently in white matter, where a male-associated myelin and axonogenesis signature accompanies reduced white matter volume in females. These molecular and structural differences coincide with elevated hippocampal microglial reactivity and an altered spatial search strategy in females, without any detectable differences in circulating markers of stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, or immunity. Together, these findings indicate that sex differences in the aging brain are expressed at the level of capillary flow regulation and regional tissue programs rather than through bulk cerebral blood flow alone, and that elevated blood flow in females can mask, rather than reflect, adequate tissue oxygenation.

pending_articles.title: Diurnal Variations in the Cholinergic System of the Nucleus Accumbens
pending_articles.content: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) plays a critical role in reward-related behaviors, which exhibit diurnal variations. Cholinergic interneurons (CINs) are the primary source of acetylcholine within the NAc and regulate local dopamine (DA) signaling through nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs). Although there are diurnal variations in NAc dynamics, little is known about whether CIN activity and nicotinic signaling also vary across the light/dark cycle. Here, we aimed to determine diurnal variations in the NAc cholinergic system using ex vivo fast-scan cyclic voltammetry and cell-attached electrophysiological recordings in male rodents. We examined time-of-day-dependent differences in nAChR-mediated modulation of DA release, spontaneous CIN firing frequency, and firing patterns. We found that spontaneous CIN firing varied across the light/dark cycle, with increased activity during the dark cycle. Additionally, bath application of nicotine (NIC), mecamylamine (MEC), and dihydro-{beta}-erythroidine (DH{beta}E) reduced CIN firing frequency during the dark cycle, with only MEC decreasing firing frequency in the light cycle. NIC and MEC also altered CIN firing patterns during the dark cycle, whereas DH{beta}E primarily affected firing frequency. Together, these findings demonstrate diurnal variations in NAc CIN activity and reveal time-of-day-dependent differences in the effects of nAChR modulation on spontaneous firing. These results suggest that nicotinic signaling may contribute to diurnal regulation of NAc cholinergic activity, providing insight into mechanisms underlying time-of-day-dependent changes in reward circuitry.

pending_articles.title: Functional characterization of the 26RFa/orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamic area reveals their key role in the control of glucose homeostasis
pending_articles.content: Defining the nature and molecular mechanisms of the neurocircuitry controlling glucose homeostasis is crucial in understanding how alterations in these pathways promote the development of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Here, we functionally characterize a population of lateral hypothalamic neurons co-expressing the anti-hyperglycemic neuropeptides 26RFa and orexin. Using complementary chemogenetic, pharmacological and genetic approaches, including mice deficient for 26RFa, orexin or both neuropeptides, we investigated the respective contribution of each signaling system to glucose homeostasis. We found that lateral hypothalamic 26RFa neurons extensively co-express orexin, defining a distinct peptidergic population with convergent anti-hyperglycemic properties. Unexpectedly, chemogenetic activation of these neurons potentiated glucose-induced hyperglycemia despite the anti-hyperglycemic properties of both neuropeptides. To understand this paradox, we examined the transcriptional responses of the 26RFa and orexin peptidergic systems and found that neuronal activation was associated with coordinated, glycemic state-dependent downregulation of both signaling systems. Furthermore, genetic loss-of-function approaches revealed distinct contributions of the two neuropeptidergic systems, with orexin signaling mediating most of the metabolic consequences of neuronal activation, whereas 26RFa signaling is required for the dynamic regulation of orexin expression. Finally, our findings provide new insights into the functional organization of lateral hypothalamic 26RFa/orexin neurons and advance our understanding of how coordinated neuropeptidergic signaling contributes to systemic glucose homeostasis.

pending_articles.title: Vibrotactile stimulation on the upper back requires stronger vibration during goal-directed reaching but does not impede reaching performance
pending_articles.content: Vibrotactile stimulation is a promising method of biofeedback, with potential applications for ergonomic posture and balance, rehabilitation, and motor learning. These applications require balancing tactile perception with motor performance and cognitive workload. In this study, participants performed a detection task, a reaching task, and a concurrent reach-and-detect task, with vibrotactile signals delivered on the hand or upper back. Sensitivity to stimuli, motor performance, and cognitive workload were compared for each task. Sensitivity was suppressed during movement, but this suppression was greater on hand compared to the upper back. Movement time was slowed by vibration on the hand but not the upper back. Mental workload and task complexity increased for the reach-and-detect task compared to the individual tasks. We conclude that vibrotactile feedback devices worn on the upper back do not impede motor performance, with only minor tactile suppression. This could be overcome by presenting highly salient or personalized feedback.

pending_articles.title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
pending_articles.content: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

recently_processed.title: Bilateral M1 tDCS selectively modulates dynamic large-scale brain states associated with sensorimotor control relative to sham stimulation
Multisensory interplay and theories of consciousness.
recently_processed.content: Sensory interplay typically refers to cases where the content of one sensory modality affects the content of another sensory modality. Although there is much evidence today of such interplay, it is unknown how to interpret them. Is it a one-way causal function between two separate states (e.g., a visual process that influences an auditory process), a bidirectional relation between two separate states, or a new kind of state—as a sensory integration—that cannot be reduced to interactions between separate states? Despite these questions, the first-person perspective offers the insight that sensory modalities often integrate and that conscious content is seldom composed exclusively of one sense. Here, we explore how to understand sensory interplay and integration and how this analysis may provide a tool to analyze and investigate theories of consciousness. We argue that multisensory interplay leads the way to new empirical approaches to theory comparison that are not derivable from research in single perceptual systems, which may suggest new potential avenues of progress in consciousness science. recently_processed.title: How ghosting and stress impact vulnerable narcissism and maladaptive daydreaming: The role of mindfulness and rumination.
recently_processed.content: The present study aims to explore the influence of ghosting and stress on maladaptive daydreaming and vulnerable narcissism within a multivariate framework, using mindfulness and rumination as mediators. We employed a cross-sectional design and conducted it among 301 university students (Mage = 20.07; SDage = 1.83) in Vietnam. The study utilized the Maladaptive Daydreaming Scale, Hypersensitive Narcissism Scale, Rumination Response Scale, Mindful Attention Awareness Scale, Perceived Stress Scale, and the Ghosting Questionnaire. A multivariate structural equation model was utilized for the analysis. The findings indicated that both stress and ghosting positively influenced maladaptive daydreaming and vulnerable narcissism. Mindfulness and rumination were identified as mediators of the influence of stress and ghosting on vulnerable narcissism, while only mindfulness served as a mediator of the influence of stress and ghosting on maladaptive daydreaming. These findings highlight significant implications for alleviating the adverse effects of stress and ghosting on maladaptive daydreaming and vulnerable narcissism through mindfulness interventions and educational support programs. However, the study’s design limitations pose challenges in establishing causal conclusions. This suggests the need for more robust designs, such as longitudinal and experimental studies, to test the relationships and evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed interventions. recently_processed.title: The conscious experience of thinking aloud: Are positive feelings associated with better think-aloud performance?
recently_processed.content: The think-aloud interview is a psychological procedure used to measure an individual’s cognition in solving a task. However, very little is known about how an individual’s conscious experience of the interview might be associated with their performance during the interview. This is consequential as data derived from think-aloud studies are often used to validate high-stakes educational cognitive tasks. This study primarily explored the relationship between an individuals’ conscious experience during the think-aloud interview and their problem-solving accuracy. Sixty-six undergraduate students, enrolled in a teacher education program, were invited to think aloud as they solved four math tasks. Students were also invited to complete a series of surveys to measure the aspects of their conscious experience, including attitudes, motivation, and feelings, about the think-aloud interview. Regression analyses revealed that participants who had more positive conscious experiences about the think-aloud interview as measured by global direct feelings about the interview exhibited more accurate problem solving than those who had less-positive conscious experiences of the interview. Moreover, students who reported higher intrinsic motivation for the tasks and less-negative affective attitudes about making mistakes tended to report better conscious experiences about the thinking aloud interview. The continued use of this method with cautions about the conscious experience of participants is discussed. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

recently_processed.title: Mystical experiences in virtual reality.
recently_processed.content: Virtual reality (VR) has shown promise as a psychological means of inducing mystical experiences. Here, we compared the subjective responses of 48 undergraduate volunteers to script-guided multiuser perceptual experiences in VR (VR perception [VR-P]) with their responses to a control condition involving guided imagery while their eyes were closed (eyes-closed imagery). Nineteen participants (40%) met the criteria for a “complete” mystical experience in response to VR-P on the Mystical Experiences Questionnaire–30 (MEQ-30), while only three (5%) achieved this in response to eyes-closed imagery. VR-P was also more evocative of a sense of presence, vividness, and absorption, as well as various positive affective experiences, most prominent among which included awe, beauty, and being mindfully observant, but also novelty, interest, contentment, and joy. Comparably, negative affective responses were rarely reported even at a very low intensity. Guided perception in VR of a beautiful, realistic environment also inclusive of awe-provocative, surrealistic elements thus could be an effective method to induce mystical experiences in at least a sizable minority of participants.
